catalog.description: Domain-pattern vac fatigues remain the working uniform of crews, militias, and cash-poor infantry. Local factories preserve the seals; unrestricted movement comes at the price of dangerous exposure.

Cordon shells are obsolete station-security cuirasses sold after their seals, shock liners, or liability tags fail inspection. A local armorer can make one wearable again, but mismatched plates and tired joints leave the user with protection no professional force would call dependable.

A Lashplate harness is a cargo frame, pressure web, and slabs of whatever a breaker crew could drill and wire into place. The mass can catch fragments and weak rounds, but crude balance, exposed lines, and almost nonexistent material matching make it cheap protection for expendable hands.
Kazeron's Bastion pattern lets League member worlds replace one another's plates and seals. Layered laminate trades modest mobility for dependable coalition line protection.

Tri-Tachyon's Aegis exchanges thick conventional plate for laminated composites, predictive threat displays, and powered balance correction. It cannot absorb a slugging match like Legionary armor, but it moves quickly and presents a difficult firing solution.

integralSystem.description: The same threat display that buys the Aegis its footing can just as easily lock a firing solution. When the wearer holds a clear line on something worth spending it on, the suit's shoulder pod puts a brace of smart micro-missiles into it before the wearer would otherwise get a shot off. The rack is small, it is not the wearer's rifle, and it does not refill in the field.

catalog.description: Church armorers rebuild Palatine suits from inherited pressure shells, hand-fitted ceramic, and carefully husbanded powered joints. The result is slow and laborious to maintain, but unusually resistant once a sanctioned guardian sets their feet.

Sindrian Furnace armor surrounds a conventional pressure frame with thick petrochemical laminate and conspicuous state fittings. It carries more sacrificial plate than its peers, while heat, weight, and an unsubtle silhouette punish prolonged maneuver.

A Reaver rig is a Blackforge frame that survived long enough to acquire powered bracing and another generation of ship plate. It is fast for its bulk and can soak punishment, but poor material matching gives penetrators few reasons to stop.
Tri-Tachyon's Janus suit hides composite segments beneath a sensor hood and electronic-warfare weave. Corporate scouts prize its speed; gray-market users struggle with the interfaces.

integralSystem.description: The hood's sensor cluster and the weave under the plate normally idle at whatever the licence permits. Held at the edge of ground the scout cannot see into, the suit spends its whole thermal budget on one wide active return and puts the result straight onto the company net: the room, the street, and a short way through the nearer walls, for as long as the emitters can stand it. It is proprietary, it is expensive to run, and it tells you what is there. It does nothing else.

catalog.description: The XIV heavy battlesuit is the Hegemony's Domain-spec answer to a breach: dense ceramic, powered bracing, and standardized hardpoints. It survives punishment at an obvious cost in speed.

integralSystem.description: Domain-spec bracing driven off the suit's own plant, on a doctrine timer rather than a gamble. It carries the wearer through the threshold at a pace the Hegemony can train, repeat, and account for, with the frontal plate locked forward the whole way. Nothing about it is improvised, which is the entire point.

catalog.description: The Specter is a corporate breach shell built around high-output joints, composite armor, and continuous threat prediction. It gives up the XIV pattern's raw staying power to cross exposed ground faster and remain unexpectedly elusive for a walking tank.

integralSystem.description: The threat display picks the moment and the joints spend everything on it. The window is short and comes around again quickly; the screen is a courtesy rather than a wall. Corporate doctrine holds that the fastest way through a killing ground is to not be standing in it.

catalog.description: The League's Bulwark program favors modular plate blocks, replaceable actuators, and control standards that member worlds can reproduce. It lacks any one spectacular advantage and instead preserves credible protection, handling, and coalition repairability together.

integralSystem.description: Coalition breaching drill rendered in hardware: the actuators surge and the shoulder blocks interlock outward, covering a wider front than one wearer strictly needs. Member worlds standardized on the wider arc because the marine beside you may not be from your navy.

catalog.description: Each Reliquary shell is an artisan-restored legacy machine entrusted only to a Knight who has passed the Church's trials of custody. Dense fitted armor turns aside heavy fire, but conservative governors and immense mass make the wearer deliberate rather than swift.

integralSystem.description: The custody governors release and the shell walks forward behind its own fitted plate, unhurried, for a long time. A Knight in this suit is not crossing the room quickly. They are crossing it in front of somebody else.

catalog.description: Lion's Mantle suits carry thick Sindrian laminates, oversized cooling loops, and enough polished state ornament to make concealment irrelevant. Privileged logistics buy an enormous armor reserve; weight and silhouette leave the operator dependent on a disciplined advance.

integralSystem.description: The cooling loops dump everything they have been hoarding and the guard suit advances gleaming, plate spread wide. It is a magnificent thing to walk behind and an unmissable thing to shoot at, and the loops take a very long time to forgive it.

catalog.description: Foundry-breakers begin as cargo exoskeletons and end beneath welded ship plate, illicit servos, and whatever shock padding a raider cell can steal. The crude mass takes extraordinary punishment before coming apart, but offers poor resistance and nearly no tactical grace.

integralSystem.description: Industrial shoulder rams and a salvaged riot screen, wired to the same trigger by somebody in a hurry. It fires hard enough to throw the rig through a doorway and no further, the screen is a sheet of scrap, and the servos need a long sulk afterwards. The flanks are exactly as exposed as they always were.

catalog.description: Blackforge rig means cut-down security armor, industrial exoframe, ship plate, and hand-fitted seals from pirate or Pather shops. No two suits agree; the better examples are quick and stubborn.
The Hegemony's Legionary suit favors interchangeable plates, pressure integrity, and field-serviceable joints. It is heavier than scout gear and built for disciplined formations far from a depot.
Ward is the frontier name for locally assembled torso plate, sealed helmet, and available impact layers. Stations, Church villages, and auxiliaries issue it to section leaders.

The Hegemony does not buy corporate sensor suits; it strips a Legionary down to the frame and hangs a surveying array off it. The Pathfinder is heavier, louder, and far easier to fix than anything Tri-Tachyon sells a scout, and an auxiliary can be taught to run one in a fortnight.

integralSystem.description: A mapping array asked to do something it was not sold for. It reads further than a Janus hood and holds the return longer, because it is bigger and the Hegemony does not mind that it announces itself doing so. Everyone within a few streets knows a survey sweep happened. Doctrine treats that as somebody else's problem.

catalog.description: One League member world builds the shell, another the array, a third the endurance pack, and the coalition argues about the interfaces for a decade. What comes out is a scout suit a section can live in for a week, and that puts everything it sees on a net six navies can read.

integralSystem.description: The deepest active return anyone fields, and the only one built to be shared rather than owned. It opens the ground ahead, reads well past the nearer walls, and recovers quickly enough that an outrider can spend it twice crossing one street. What it costs is the pack, the weight, and the certainty that anybody listening heard it.

catalog.description: Hegemony siege issue: Legionary plate with every weight limit taken off, because the marine wearing it is not expected to go anywhere. It is what holds a breach once the assault sections have made one, and it is miserable to walk any distance in.

Corporate security surplus, sold by the container to anyone who will take it. It was built to walk a picket line into a crowd, so it has a real shield and almost no assist worth the name -- and it turns out a station corridor is not so different from a picket line.

integralSystem.description: The shield comes up and the frame locks behind it. That is the whole system: no shove, no crossing speed, nothing a breach family would recognise as an assist. What it does have is a genuine shield, which covers a narrow slice of one direction and covers it better than a suit this cheap has any right to.

catalog.description: An unpowered cargo frame with the load arms cut short and a launch rail welded where a crate used to sit. Independent crews build them because a section that can put one rocket into a bunker is worth more than a section that cannot, and because the frame was already in the hold.

integralSystem.description: One missile, on a rail, aimed by the wearer turning to face the thing. There is no threat display and there is no second round: the frame carries what it was loaded with in the hold, and the crew decided which target was worth it before the drop. Often they decided wrong.

catalog.description: The Hegemony's answer to carrying the heavy thing: a powered suit built around the rack rather than a suit with a rack added to it. It is slower than a Legionary and worth every second of that, because the section walking with it can ask for indirect fire and get it from inside the room.

integralSystem.description: Four rounds in the rack and a doctrine for spending them. Where the Aegis waits for a firing solution its own display likes, the Arbalest waits for a target its section commander would call worth a missile, and then sends more of them than the Aegis carries in total. It is not cleverer. It is a battery.

catalog.description: Diktat state security orders these by the crate for work its own citizens are not supposed to hear about. It is a riot shell built up until it can take a rifle round rather than a thrown brick -- heavier than the pattern it descends from, lighter than anything the Lion's Guard would deign to wear, and issued to people expected to go through a door on a schedule.

integralSystem.description: A shield and a shove, both adequate, neither remarkable. It is the version of the idea a state can afford to issue to everybody, and it is worth exactly what the Diktat pays for it: enough to get a section through a doorway that a riot shell would not have survived, and nowhere near enough to make that pleasant.
